title: Checking AI Materials for Accuracy and Bias

production_notes: No facts to verify: content.md Review Flags say None. The science fact used (plants take in carbon dioxide for photosynthesis) is standard school content.
Leila and her primary school in Amman are fictional; stock footage must show no real school name, crest or logo.
The story and question details on the slides are invented for the example; the slides do not reproduce any real AI output.
The analogy scene mentions allergies only as a general idea; show a neutral kitchen scene with no medical claims.

Hook.voiceover: An AI-generated story reads well, and the questions look fine. But if every character comes from one culture, every doctor is a man, or one date is wrong, your learners will notice. Some will learn the error. Others will feel it is not for them.

Explain.voiceover: Last time, we made materials accessible. Now we check them for accuracy and bias. AI assistants learn from large amounts of existing text. That text contains errors, old information, and the same stereotypes that exist in society. So AI materials can contain them too.

slide.title: Checking AI Materials for Accuracy and Bias
slide.body: AI for Educators and Trainers · Lesson 8 of 12. Subtitle: What goes in comes out.

Explain.voiceover: Watch for five kinds of problem. Factual errors, often written confidently. Outdated information, like rules that have changed. Cultural stereotypes, such as certain jobs always linked to one gender. Exclusion, where names, foods or family types come from only one culture. And poor fit, with the wrong level or content that does not match your curriculum or procedures.

slide.title: What can go wrong
slide.body: Factual errors · Outdated information · Cultural stereotypes · Exclusion: one culture only · Poor fit: level, curriculum, procedures

Explain.voiceover: So use a five-part review on every AI material before learners see it. Facts: is every fact, number and definition correct? Check against a reliable source, like your textbook or an official procedure. Level: is the language right for these learners?

slide.title: 5-part review checklist
slide.body: Five boxes in a row: Facts (check a reliable source) · Level · Cultural fairness · Representation · Curriculum fit. First two highlighted.

Explain.voiceover: Cultural fairness: are people and places shown respectfully, without stereotypes? Representation: do the examples include a range of names, genders, backgrounds, abilities and family types? Could all your learners see themselves here? And curriculum fit: does it match your outcome and syllabus? For quiz questions, also check there is exactly one correct answer.

slide.title: 5-part review checklist
slide.body: Same five boxes; last three highlighted: Cultural fairness · Representation ('Could every learner see themselves here?') · Curriculum fit. Extra tag for quizzes: exactly one correct answer.

Explain.voiceover: You can also ask the AI to list stereotypes or one-sided examples in its own text. This can find some problems. But it does not replace your own review, because the same patterns that created a problem can also hide it.

slide.title: Ask AI to review, then review yourself
slide.body: List any stereotypes or one-sided examples in this text.  → useful, but not a replacement for your own review

Explain.voiceover: Reviewing AI materials is like checking food before you serve it to guests. It may look good on the plate, but you still check it is cooked, fresh, and safe for a guest with an allergy. You check because you are the one serving it.
Explain.stock_query: cook tasting food before serving guests
Explain.on_screen_text: You are the one serving it

Demonstrate.voiceover: Let's go back to a primary classroom. Leila teaches Year Four at a primary school in Amman, in Jordan. She asks an AI assistant for a short story about a class preparing a science fair, with five comprehension questions.
Demonstrate.stock_query: primary school children science fair project

Demonstrate.voiceover: She starts with facts. The story says plants use oxygen to make their food. That is wrong. In photosynthesis they use carbon dioxide, so she corrects it. Then level. Two sentences are too long for nine-year-olds, so she splits them.

slide.title: Facts and level
slide.body: Before (red): 'Plants use oxygen to make their food.' After (green): 'Plants use carbon dioxide to make their food.' Level: two long sentences → split for 9-year-olds.

Demonstrate.voiceover: Next, fairness and representation. All six children's names come from one culture, and the only child who is good at science is a boy. Leila changes the names to reflect the range of backgrounds in her school and in the wider world. And she makes a girl the child who explains the experiment.

slide.title: Fairness and representation
slide.body: Before: six names from one culture; only a boy is good at science. After: names from a range of backgrounds; a girl explains the experiment.

Demonstrate.voiceover: Curriculum fit. The story mentions a topic her class will not study until next year, so she removes it. And question four asks why the team won, but the story gives two possible reasons. She rewrites it, so there is one clear answer.

slide.title: Fit and questions
slide.body: Next year's topic → removed · Question 4 'Why did the team win?' had two answers → rewritten with one clear answer

Demonstrate.voiceover: She records each change in a small table, so she can see patterns and write better prompts next time. For example, use a range of names from different cultures.

slide.title: Leila's change log
slide.body: Table: Location | Type | Correction. Rows: fact, level, representation, fit, question. Footer: next prompt adds 'use a range of names from different cultures'.

Demonstrate.voiceover: A common mistake is to check only the facts and stop there. Bias is harder to see, especially when the material matches our own background. So ask: who is missing, and who is always in the same role? And asking for diverse examples does not guarantee a fair result.
Demonstrate.on_screen_text: Who is missing? Who is stuck?

Recap.voiceover: Let's recap. First, AI materials can contain factual errors, outdated information, stereotypes, and examples that exclude some learners. Second, use a five-part review before learners see anything: facts, level, cultural fairness, representation and curriculum fit. Third, AI can point out possible problems, but it does not replace your review, and a good prompt does not guarantee a fair result.

slide.title: Key takeaways
slide.body: 1. Errors, outdated facts, stereotypes, exclusion. 2. Facts · Level · Fairness · Representation · Fit. 3. AI helps; your review decides.

CTA.voiceover: Now it is your turn. In the exercise below this video, ask AI for a short reading passage and five questions on a topic you know well, describing your learners only as a group. Review them with the checklist, record every error or bias, and write a corrected version. Next week, your capstone begins. In the next lesson, we build quizzes with AI and Google Forms. See you there.
